source.title: L$^2$M: Mutual Information Scaling Law for Long-Context Language Modeling
source.authors: Zhuo Chen; Oriol Mayn'e i Comas; Zhuo-Tao Jin; Di Luo; Marin Soljačić

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports mutual-information scaling and long-context modeling results, but explicitly distinguishes its question from neural scaling laws. It does not test held-out loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. as prior neural-scaling-law work and says its question is distinct. Its own results concern bipartite mutual information versus sequence length and long-context KL/NLL across architectures, not the claim's loss-versus-size, data, or compute relationships. Those adjacent results are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper measures bipartite mutual information versus sequence length using LLMs as density estimators, and long-context KL/NLL across GPT2 and Mamba at varying sequence length and model size. It explicitly says this is distinct from neural scaling laws (loss vs model size, data, compute at fixed context). No held-out loss is fitted against parameters, tokens or compute, no extrapolation, allocation or fixed-parameter shape comparison is made, and there is no downstream-task evaluation. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that natural-language bipartite mutual information follows a sub-volume power law in sequence length. Effective long-context modeling therefore requires history-state dimension to grow at least as fast (the L2M condition): transformers satisfy it as single models, while fixed-state SSMs need model size to grow with length. They state this is distinct from neural scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The paper estimates mutual information and evaluates long-context KL/NLL across sequence lengths and architectures; it does not fit the held-out-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation studied by the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different estimators (bias-corrected direct and vCLUB), datasets, density-estimator models, and partition ratios for mutual-information measurements. Long-context results also vary by architecture, model size, sequence length, and token position.

fits_no_version.finding: Bipartite mutual information between adjacent text halves grows as a power law in sequence length on PG19 and Wikipedia. This holds with LLaMA 3.1 405B and DeepSeek V3 Base, two estimators, and several split ratios. The authors say the exponent is likely underestimated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bipartite mutual information in natural language grows sub-volume (L^beta, beta<1) with sequence length.

fits_no_version.finding: Mamba KL on synthetic Gaussian data collapses onto a single curve against I_BP/dim(z), across 50M–1.4B parameters and 64–16,384 lengths. GPT2 KL stays stable across lengths. On PG19, Mamba NLL plateaus at late positions, and the gap to GPT2 narrows with size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Long-context modeling quality depends on history-state size relative to the data's bipartite mutual information (L2M condition).

record.problems: The paper states that both mutual-information estimators likely underestimate the true exponent; its synthetic Gaussian validation may not capture all natural-language complexity; and it relies primarily on open-source models. Several reported numerical results appear only in figures.

untested.parts: All: no loss-vs-parameters/tokens/compute power-law fit; model size varies only within long-context KL/NLL comparisons.
All: no extrapolation of fitted loss laws to larger runs.
All: GPT2 vs Mamba comparisons are not at matched parameter count, and the measure is long-context position-wise behaviour, not a shape ablation.
All: the synthetic Gaussian KL results do not fit power laws in model scale.
All: no downstream tasks evaluated; the authors list this as an open question.
All: estimator dependence concerns the mutual-information exponent, not neural scaling-law exponents.

record.verdict_notes: Row links (all ['none']) and cannot_determine states are appropriate, since none measures a version's effect. r6 size_stated mixes Mamba and Mamba2 ranges, which is a minor issue. r1/r2 both cite the same Fig. 2(b) panel, which is fine. The two-point mutual information decay result (Fig. 2c, B.4) is unrecorded but is also irrelevant to every version.
